analysis.one_liner: Gives tax breaks to small grocery stores opening in areas with little competition, to help lower food prices.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee since its January 2025 introduction, with only 2 cosponsors and no committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give federal tax breaks to small, independent food retailers — grocery stores with under $200 million in annual sales — that open or operate in counties where a few chains control most of the grocery market. It creates a 15% credit for a new store's start-up investments and sweetens several existing tax breaks for these businesses, including credits for hiring workers and rehabilitating buildings. The idea is that more grocery competitors in concentrated markets would pressure prices down for shoppers.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main direct beneficiaries would be small and independent grocers opening or operating stores in counties with highly concentrated grocery markets, who would receive a new 15% investment credit and larger versions of existing business tax breaks. Residents of those areas would benefit indirectly, and only if the new competition actually materialized and pushed prices down.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small grocers in areas with few competitors

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new tax credit worth 15% of the capital investment (property, facilities, equipment) made by a new small food retail business in its first years of operation.

Raises the historic-rehabilitation tax credit from 20% to 25%, the work-opportunity hiring credit limits by $2,000-$6,000 per worker, the bonus depreciation rate by 10 percentage points, and the pass-through business income deduction from 20% to 25% — but only for qualifying small food retail businesses.

Qualifying businesses must have gross receipts of $200 million or less, get at least 70% of receipts from retail food or produce sales, and be located in a county where grocery retail concentration (as measured by USDA's Herfindahl-Hirschman Index) is at or above 1,400.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through foregone revenue. The bill raises no offsetting revenue; the cost of the new credits and expanded breaks would add to the deficit or be paid for elsewhere in a future tax bill.

drawbacks.text: The benefit to shoppers is indirect and not guaranteed: the bill subsidizes small grocers' startup and operating costs, but nothing in it requires lower shelf prices, so the tax savings could simply flow to the store owners.

The 1,400 concentration threshold is not very strict — many ordinary suburban and rural counties with normally competitive retail would qualify — so the credits could subsidize businesses that would have opened anyway, at cost to the Treasury.

Food prices are driven by many factors beyond local retail competition (wholesale costs, transport, processing concentration), so even successful entry of small grocers would have a modest effect on overall prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The intent — more grocery competition in areas where a few chains dominate — addresses a real problem for shoppers. But the design leans on an unproven chain of events: subsidize small stores, hope they open, hope competition lowers prices. Without any price discipline or revenue offset, the likeliest outcome is a windfall for some small grocers with uncertain benefit to shoppers, and a modest cost to federal revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it; it has no scheduled hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mikie Sherrill introduced the bill on January 23, 2025, joined by Rep. Jahana Hayes, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill has 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, and no Republicans have signed on.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — has been taken on the bill since its referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost materially. The concentrated grocery chains that dominate qualifying counties simply retain their position, while shoppers there see no change; the bill sits untouched in committee.

for.name: Rep. Mikie Sherrill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats have supported the bill so far, and no one has voted on or publicly opposed it, so the partisan shape is not yet established.

industries.note: These businesses would receive a new 15% investment credit and expanded versions of four existing tax breaks. Shoppers benefit only insofar as the subsidy leads to more stores and lower prices.

industries.industry: Large grocery chains and dominant local supermarket operators
industries.note: The bill imposes no direct cost on them, but its stated purpose is to foster competitors in the counties where they hold the most market power, which would pressure their prices and margins. Their interest in keeping local dominance runs against shoppers' interest in lower prices.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action five months after introduction, only 2 cosponsors, and no bipartisan support, the bill is very unlikely to advance on its own. Its provisions could conceivably be folded into a broader tax package in Ways and Means, but as a standalone bill it is headed for the common fate of dying quietly in committee at the end of the Congress.
